A research paper, explained for everyone

Edit an AI photo with a dial: each change is an arrow, kept to the spot where it belongs

SphereEdit turns text edits like “glasses” or “old” into equal-length directions inside Stable Diffusion, blends them by turning an angle, and uses the model's own attention maps to keep each edit mostly in its own region, with no retraining.

Based on the paper: SphereEdit: Spherical Semantic Editing in Diffusion Models · Salamata Konate, Hassan Hamidi, Elham Dolatabadi, Frank Rudzicz, Laleh Seyyed-Kalantri · WACV (Open Access version, Computer Vision Foundation)

🧒 In kid words

Imagine a magic dial for a photo. Turn it one way and the person looks older, turn it the other way and they look younger, or stop partway to mix in a second change like glasses. The computer also tries to keep each change in its own spot, like glasses on the eyes.

📖 The short version

AI image editors often change more than you asked for: add lipstick and the skin tone shifts too. SphereEdit treats every requested change as an arrow of the same length, so you can mix two changes just by picking an angle. It uses the AI's own sense of where each word 'looks' in the picture to keep edits from spreading. It works on an existing model without any extra training.

🔬 For experts

Attribute directions are unit-normalized noise-prediction differences v_k = ε_θ(z_t,t,c_k) − ε_θ(z_t,t,c∅). They are composed with spherical coefficients (cos θ, sin θ cos ϕ, sin θ sin ϕ) and added to the base prediction inside the DDIM update of Stable Diffusion v1.5. Token-specific cross-attention maps, thresholded at quantile q, localize each direction, and a masked Gram–Schmidt projection decorrelates directions only where their regions overlap. On 100 FFHQ images it leads CLIP-I and DINO on both compositional edits tested against SEGA, Composable Diffusion, Cycle Diffusion and TurboEdit.

Why it matters: Uses the paper names, such as creative design, virtual try-on and content creation, need edits that are precise, can be combined, and leave the rest of the image alone. SphereEdit gets them from an off-the-shelf diffusion model with an easy-to-read angle control, instead of slow per-image optimization or retraining.

0.1436 LPIPS on Eyebrow+Lipstick (SEGA 0.1870; lower means fewer artifacts) (source: Table 1)

Why does asking for glasses change the whole face?

In one sentence: Earlier AI editors often change things you never asked for, and that is the problem SphereEdit attacks.

Ask a diffusion model to add "glasses" to a photo, and you may get more than glasses, as with this earlier method, Composable Diffusion.

From the paper · Figure 3

See it: one request, several changes

Drag the divider to compare the original with the 'Glasses' edit.

What to notice: the glasses arrive, but so do stubble on the chin (1) and a greenish background (2). Nobody asked.

The paper's own example of this leaking is "lipstick" that also changes skin tone Abstract. For uses the paper names, such as creative design, virtual try-on and content creation, edits must keep the person the same Sec. 1.

🧒 Explain it like I'm 8

Picture a dial with an arrow on it. Every edit is an arrow of the same length: "glasses" points one way, "young" another. To mix them, turn the dial to point in between. Each arrow paints only its own spot: glasses on the eyes, lipstick on the lips.

Inside the model, each word becomes an edit arrow: the change in the AI's guess about what to clean away when that word is added. Every arrow is first resized to length 1, so no edit wins just because it is naturally bigger. An angle sets each edit's share of the mix; a separate strength knob sets how strong it is. Each arrow acts mainly where its word "looks" in the picture Sec. 3.2. It needs no retraining: the photo is turned back into noise and rebuilt with an existing model (Stable Diffusion v1.5) Sec. 4.1, with the edit slipped in during the rebuilding steps you choose (each attribute can be switched on only for part of the process; see "Inside one step") Sec. 3.1, 3.2.

Toy example

Try it: free knobs vs. one dial

Turn the dial, then try the two free knobs and push both up.

What to notice: with the dial, the tip slides along the circle. Free knobs can push it past the outer ring, where the picture over-saturates Sec. 3. The paper says real edit arrows are only roughly at right angles, so in practice the total would only approximately follow the circle (our inference; the paper doesn't measure this).

One dial, two edits: steering a face by angle

In one sentence: Two edit arrows get shares set by one angle (cos θ and sin θ), so picking the mix is just turning a dial, and turning to the far side pushes an edit backwards.

On the dial from above, put 'Old' pointing right and 'Asian' pointing up. You set one angle \(\theta\). The share of 'Old' is \(\cos\theta\) and the share of 'Asian' is \(\sin\theta\). The two shares trade off: more of one means less of the other.

From the paper · Figure 1 (left)

Try it: turn the dial and watch the face

Drag the handle or the slider; the photo is the paper's nearest panel.

What to notice: at 45° the face is part older, part 'Asian'. At 180° he looks younger, though the model was only given 'old'. The paper printed only these eight angles.

Why younger? At 180° the share of 'old' is −1, so the edit subtracts the 'old' arrow and pushes away from old. The paper finds that this lands roughly on 'young' (antipodal symmetry) Sec. 4.2. For race, the paper notes, an "opposite" is not well defined Sec. 5, so it is unclear what the 270° panel shows; the paper does not discuss that panel (limitations).

From the paper · Figure 4

Try it: push one edit backwards and forwards

Pick an edit, then slide its strength from −7.5 (subtract) to +7.5 (add).

What to notice: +7.5 on 'Age' adds wrinkles; −7.5 removes them and softens the face, while the person stays recognisable Sec. 4.4.

Length 1 keeps edits fair against each other; how strong a single edit is comes from a separate strength factor. The paper uses −7.5 and +7.5 in the slider above (Figure 4), and factors between 0 and 1 when mixing Sec. 3.2. With three edits, two angles, \(\theta\) and \(\phi\), set three shares.

What to notice: edit 1 gets +0.50; edits 2 and 3 get +0.61 each.

🔬 Go deeper: the formulas, and how 1D, 2D and 3D fit together

Each unit direction \(\hat v_k\) is scaled by a spherical coefficient and the results are summed (Eq. 4, 5, 8):

\[ \lambda_1=\cos\theta,\quad \lambda_2=\sin\theta\cos\phi,\quad \lambda_3=\sin\theta\sin\phi,\qquad \Delta\epsilon_t=\sum_{k:\,m_k(t)=1}\lambda_k\hat v_k \]

1D: a line, \(\theta=0\), with a strength factor (negative for the opposite edit; ±7.5 in Figure 4). 2D: a circle, \((\lambda_a,\lambda_b)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), so \(\lambda_a^2+\lambda_b^2=1\). 3D: the sphere, \(\sum_k\lambda_k^2=1\). The mixed arrow has length exactly 1 only if the \(\hat v_k\) are orthogonal; the abstract claims approximate orthogonality, and Sec. 3.2 removes overlap only where two edits' regions meet.

Turning to 180° simply subtracts the 'old' noise difference, much like steering away from a prompt in classifier-free guidance; the paper's observation is that this lands roughly on 'young'.

The "sphere" is only the span of 2–3 unit directions inside a huge noise-prediction space, not a claim that the whole latent is a sphere. The paper cites studies indicating diffusion latents are approximately spherical [9, 13] and a related VAE result [36]; it does not prove this itself. It tests at most three attributes Sec. 5.

Sec. 4.1 says θ = ϕ = π/2 activates all attributes, but by Eq. 4 that setting gives (0, 0, 1); the paper does not explain the gap, so the exact default weighting is unclear.

Inside one step: find the arrow, find its spot

In one sentence: At every step, SphereEdit asks "what changes if I say 'glasses'?" and applies that change mainly where the model looks for glasses.

The photo is first turned back into noise (DDIM inversion), then cleaned over 50 steps Sec. 4.1. At each cleanup step the model guesses what noise to remove; SphereEdit compares that guess with and without the word (one extra network pass per attribute).

Toy example

Try it: one cleanup step, five moves

Click Next. Each grid is a pretend picture; dashed boxes are the eyes.

grey = noise guess push toward 'glasses' push away attention mask

Toy built on the paper's images · Figure 5(b)

Try it: where does the edit belong?

Through cross-attention, each word "looks at" parts of the image Sec. 3.2 (3). Pick a word; drag the slider.

What to notice: 'glasses' is a sharp band at the eyes; 'lipstick' attention is weaker and more diffuse, which the paper says makes it more sensitive to the threshold Sec. 4.4.

The paper's mask cut-off is a quantile threshold q. In its Figure 5, q = 1 means no mask and q = 0 an empty mask; the authors use q = 0.8, which they find "offers the best compromise between edit strength and spatial precision" Sec. 4.4.

From the paper · Figure 5(a)

The real edits ('glasses' + 'lipstick') at different q

Pick two images; drag the divider.

What to notice: with no mask (q = 1.0) lipstick tints the skin; at q = 0.5 it stays near the lips.

This is the guard the Composable Diffusion edit at the top lacked.

Where two edits claim the same pixels (say mouth and beard), SphereEdit removes the part of one edit that duplicates the other, but only in those shared pixels Sec. 3.2 (4).

Toy pairing 'lipstick' + 'beard' · Eq. 7

Try it: untangle two edits, only where they overlap

Click a pixel; drag the arrow tips (the dial's arrows from above).

What to notice: in a shared pixel, 'lipstick' ends at a right angle to 'beard'; elsewhere it is unchanged.

🔬 Go deeper: the equations and Algorithm 1

Direction (Eq. 3). At step \(t\), \(\mathbf{v}_k(t)=\epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_k)-\epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_\varnothing)\), then \(\hat{\mathbf v}_k=\mathbf v_k/\|\mathbf v_k\|_2\) to avoid scale imbalance between attributes. The paper calls this a local linearization of the denoiser in text-conditioning space; it is the same difference used in classifier-free guidance, but normalized and applied per attribute.

Overlap (Eq. 6–7). \(\mathcal R_k(t)\) = heatmap \(M_k\) thresholded at quantile \(q\); \(S_{jk}(x,y,t)=\mathbf 1[(x,y)\in\mathcal R_j(t)\cap\mathcal R_k(t)]\); \[\mathbf v_k\leftarrow\mathbf v_k-\langle\mathbf v_k,\mathbf v_j\rangle_{S_{jk}}(\mathbf v_j\odot S_{jk}),\] with \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{S_{jk}}\) a masked inner product. Compose and apply (Eq. 8–9): \(\Delta\epsilon_t=\sum_{k:\,m_k(t)=1}\lambda_k\hat{\mathbf v}_k\), \(\hat\epsilon(t)=\epsilon_{\text{base}}(t)+\Delta\epsilon_t\), replacing the denoiser output in the DDIM update; \(m_k(t)\in\{0,1\}\) is a per-attribute on/off schedule, e.g. 'glasses' only at later steps Sec. 3.2 (1).

Algorithm 1 (one step). (1) \(\epsilon_{\text{base}}\leftarrow\epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_\varnothing)\); (2–6) for each active \(a_k\): \(\mathbf v_k\leftarrow\epsilon_\theta(z_t,t,c_k)-\epsilon_{\text{base}}\), normalize, \(M_k\leftarrow\) CrossAttention\((z_t,c_k)\); (7–10) for each pair: \(S_{jk}\leftarrow\) Overlap\((M_j,M_k)\), orthogonalize; (11) \(\lambda_k\leftarrow\) SphericalCoefficients\((\theta,\phi)\); (12) \(\hat\epsilon\leftarrow\epsilon_{\text{base}}+\sum_k\lambda_k\hat{\mathbf v}_k\); (13) DDIM update to \(z_{t-1}\).

Settings and caveats. Stable Diffusion v1.5, 50 steps, \(q=0.8\), seed 0 Sec. 4.1. The equations do not show how \(M_k\) enters \(\hat{\mathbf v}_k\) outside overlaps; the text only says the masks restrict where edits apply (the toys simply zero the edit outside the mask). Eq. 7 is an exact projection only when \(\mathbf v_j\) has unit norm on the overlap, and the paper does not say whether directions are renormalized after it (Algorithm 1 normalizes at line 4, then orthogonalizes at line 9); the toy shows the idealized projection. The Figure 5 caption (q = 0 empty mask, q = 1 no mask) and the ablation text (low thresholds give broad masks, q > 0.8 prunes too aggressively) describe q in opposite directions; the images match the caption. The abstract says directions "modulate cross-attention activations", while Sec. 3 adds them to the noise prediction; this page follows Sec. 3.

Does it actually edit more cleanly? And where are the limits?

In one sentence: On the paper's face tests, SphereEdit keeps the picture closest to the original on most scores, though not on every one.

The authors compared SphereEdit (run on Stable Diffusion v1.5) with four earlier editing methods that use inversion, attention control or latent directions: SEGA, Composable Diffusion, Cycle Diffusion and TurboEdit Sec. 4, Table 1. You saw Composable Diffusion leak on plain "Glasses" at the top; here is how each copes with three.

From the paper · Figure 3

Try it: same face, five editors

Pick an edit and a method; drag the divider.

What to notice: Composable Diffusion's face turns pale and thinner on a greenish background. SphereEdit's multi-edit rows are not leak-free either (some stubble and background change, subtle lipstick); the paper calls its edits better localized Sec. 4.2.

On 100 FFHQ face photos, each method made two combined edits Sec. 4.3. Four automatic scores judged them: three from other AI models (CLIP and DINO) and one perceptual-difference measure (LPIPS):

  • CLIP-T: does the image match the requested words?
  • CLIP-I: does the picture still look like the original overall?
  • DINO: are the shapes and layout kept?
  • LPIPS: how much do texture and color differ? Lower is better.
From the paper · Table 1

Try it: one score at a time

Choose a task and a score (each score has its own scale).

What to notice: on Glasses + Mustache, SphereEdit's DINO (0.7026) is clearly ahead of SEGA (0.6271) and Composable Diffusion (0.3226), while CLIP-T spans only 0.2203 to 0.2369. SphereEdit is not best everywhere: SEGA wins LPIPS there, and TurboEdit edges it on CLIP-T for Eyebrow + Lipstick Table 1.

A full three-attribute edit takes about 12 seconds on one NVIDIA L40 GPU Sec. 4.1. The paper reports no timings for the baselines, so no speed comparison is possible.

How firm are these numbers? They come from a single fixed seed (0) on 100 images, with no error bars, and the paper does not state which backbone or settings each baseline used Sec. 4.1, 4.3.

Keep in mind:

  • Automatic scores on faces, two edit pairs, one seed, no error bars, no human study.
  • At most three attributes were tested; how stable bigger mixes are is not yet clear Sec. 5.
  • "Opposite" arrows can be ill-defined: for race, or for a disease in medical images (health or another condition?) Sec. 5.

Glossary

Antipodal symmetry
The idea that the arrow pointing the exact opposite way gives roughly the opposite attribute, like 'old' versus 'young'.
Baseline
An earlier method that a new method is compared against; here SEGA, Composable Diffusion, Cycle Diffusion and TurboEdit.
CLIP-T / CLIP-I
Scores from the CLIP model measuring how well the edited image matches the requested text (T) and how similar it stays to the original subject (I); higher is better.
Cross-attention map
A heat map from inside the model showing which parts of the image a given word in the prompt is focusing on.
DDIM inversion
Running the denoising process backwards so a real photo is turned into the noise that would regenerate it, which makes the photo editable.
Denoiser (UNet)
The network inside a diffusion model that looks at a noisy image and predicts the noise to remove.
Diffusion model
An AI that makes images by starting from random noise and removing a little noise at a time until a picture appears.
DINO / LPIPS
DINO measures whether structure and layout are kept (higher is better); LPIPS measures low-level visual differences such as texture and color (lower is better).
Edit direction (edit arrow)
The difference between the model's prediction with an attribute prompt (like 'glasses') and with the null prompt, which SphereEdit rescales to length 1 before mixing: what that attribute adds.
FFHQ
A public dataset of high-quality face photos; the paper uses 100 of its images for the numeric comparison.
GPU
A graphics chip that computers use to run AI models quickly; the paper times SphereEdit on an NVIDIA L40.
Latent
A compressed version of the image that the diffusion model actually works on, decoded back into pixels at the end.
Noise prediction
The model's guess, at each cleanup step, of which noise to remove from the current image; SphereEdit edits by nudging this guess.
Null prompt
An empty text condition; the model's prediction with it serves as the 'no edit' baseline.
Orthogonalization (Gram–Schmidt)
Removing the part of one arrow that points along another, so the two no longer pull in overlapping ways.
Quantile threshold q
The cut-off used to turn an attention heat map into a yes/no region where an edit is allowed.
Scale factor (strength)
An extra multiplier on an edit arrow: between 0 and 1 when mixing edits, or larger for a single edit (Figure 4 uses −7.5 and +7.5), where a negative value pushes toward the opposite.
Spherical coefficients
Weights like cos θ and sin θ that split one fixed budget among several edits according to angles.
Stable Diffusion v1.5
The publicly available text-to-image diffusion model all of the paper's experiments use.
Training-free
Works with the existing model as is, without fine-tuning or per-image optimization.
Unit vector
An arrow of length exactly 1, so it carries only a direction, not a strength.

How this page was made

This explainer was written by a team of AI agents. A lead editor read the paper and planned the page; experts wrote the sections: Diffusion image-editing critic and results storyteller (Why does asking for glasses change the whole face?, Does it actually edit more cleanly? And where are the limits?); Spherical-geometry and latent-direction expert (One dial, two edits: steering a face by angle); Stable Diffusion internals and cross-attention localization expert (Inside one denoising step: find the arrow, find where it belongs). The page was then revised over 1 round using feedback from simulated readers (Maya, 8, reading with her dad, Jordan, 15, a high-school student, Prof. Elena Rossi, 55, a professor in the field, Margaret, 70, a retired librarian), reviews by the experts of each other's sections, and a fact-checker that compared every section with the paper.

It can still contain mistakes: the original paper is the authoritative source. Anything marked Toy example is a simplified teaching illustration with made-up numbers, not a result from the paper. Figures marked From the paper are reproduced from it.
